content:
Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and the latest cheaper non-designer styles tout built-in AI, but as far back as early July, the company announced "ridiculous" limits on free uses of an accessibility feature.

In effect, Meta retroactively paywalled a piece of hardware already sold to customers. Update: The social network now says it has "paused" the plan to put that feature behind a paywall — see the end.

Meta first began rolling out Conversation Focus back in December.

It's a clever use of AI, and one of its biggest merits is that it runs on-device — neither compromising privacy nor requiring cellular data.

However, per The Verge, Meta is now capping free usage of the feature, with additional uses requiring extra payment.

This makes it all the more unacceptable. First, as the site's reporter Sean Hollister notes, because the feature runs on-device and makes no use of Meta's servers, there is simply no reasonable justification to charge users for it. Second, it's an accessibility feature, and some users may have bought the glasses specifically for this purpose.

Top-rated comment from KJ705

It's hard to imagine paywalling accessibility will be well-received down the line.

Accessibility-adjacent: I recently bought my mom a pair of AirPods Pro 3 specifically for the hearing aid feature. I was very impressed with the hearing aid functionality, though I do wish it performed better at canceling background noise. She finds it very useful.

When The Verge reached out for comment, Meta said the limits "currently" apply only to Conversation Focus, implying that other AI features could see usage caps down the line. The company told us that because the feature is designed for people with normal hearing, it is not considered an accessibility feature. But I think that's a semantic game, because some people have a harder time following conversations in noisy environments than others.

All of which might be good news for the upcoming Apple Glasses — giving consumers one more reason, even if the up-front cost is higher, to lean toward AI smart glasses from the better-regarded company. Apple has consistently said it never demands an ROI on accessibility investments, instead treating them as a way to contribute to a better world.

Apple Glasses are expected to formally launch sometime next year.

Update: Meta told The Verge that it has paused plans to limit access to Conversation Focus, but the company hasn't abandoned the idea of paywalling some glasses features.
